conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. I know you’re feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Abdomen… big… hurts… no pain now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your belly is very swollen. We saw that in the ER. Your blood pressure was low too, but it improved after we put in a tube to help empty your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube… okay. Foot… hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll manage your foot pain. You’re on your usual pain meds. We’ll add a patch later if needed. Right now, we’re focused on your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan. It shows your colon is very dilated—like a balloon—especially in the lower part. But no blockage. We think it’s due to your chronic constipation or a sluggish bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No… blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No blockage seen. But we can’t rule out a mass yet. We’ll keep watching. We started antibiotics just in case there’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was high and you had a fever. Also, your lungs showed some changes on the scan—could be from aspiration. So we’re treating both gut and lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs… okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oxygen levels are good. No cough. But we’re being cautious. You’re on IV antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an ultrasound on your legs because one looked swollen. No blood clot—good news. But we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Swelling… gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Slight swelling remains, but no clot. You’re still on your blood thinner, so that helps prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your belly got more distended yesterday and you spiked a fever. The CT showed worse dilation. We started stronger antibiotics for a possible bowel infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever… gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fever is gone. Your white count is coming down. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics… long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to oral vancomycin for 14 days. Even though your stool test was negative, we think you might have had a gut infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your lungs again. The consolidation is still there, but you’re not coughing. We’ll finish a 7-day course with ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs… not pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But you’re at risk for aspiration due to your swallowing issues. We’re treating it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Swallow… hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, speech therapy confirmed you need thickened liquids and pureed food. And someone must supervise every meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your latest CT shows the colon is less dilated. The contrast is moving through. No perforation. This is a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your abdomen is softening. We’ll restart your bowel regimen slowly. Gastroenterology recommends adding Miralax daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Miralax… new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps draw water into the bowel. We’ll also keep enemas and stool softeners as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your X-ray today shows continued improvement. The bowel is less distended. You passed gas and had a small bowel movement—great signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Movement… good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. We’re also adding a lidocaine patch to your right foot. You said it helps the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it on daily. Apply for up to 12 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are improving. White count is normal. No signs of infection. We’re almost done with the pneumonia antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics… stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two more days of cipro. But you’ll continue vancomycin by mouth for two weeks to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding your iron pills for now. Infection can interfere with absorption. Restart in two weeks with your doctor’s okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Iron… later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your hemoglobin is stable. No need to rush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another X-ray shows continued improvement. Your bowel is almost back to normal size. You had another bowel movement yesterday—excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow. You’ll go back to your care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your extended care facility. They’ll continue your care with the new meds and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. Your abdomen is soft, you’re passing stool, and labs are normal. We’re discharging you with instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue vancomycin for 14 days, cipro for two more doses, Miralax daily, and the lidocaine patch. Keep thickened liquids and pureed food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: List… okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And follow up with your doctor. They’ll check on the pending stool test and schedule a colonoscopy in six weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Colonoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to make sure there’s no mass causing the dilation. But for now, you’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your back ulcers. Keep using the special mattress, turn every few hours, and moisturize your skin twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And when you sit up, use the cushion and don’t stay seated more than an hour at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. The nurse will go over your meds and discharge papers now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because your belly was very swollen and you were scheduled for a colonoscopy that got delayed. Is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My stomach is big, but not painful. I haven’t felt sick or vomited.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I see you have a history of stroke and chronic constipation. Your family mentioned you’ve had this bloating before. We’re going to check things with some scans to make sure there’s no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain. Just full feeling. I did take some magnesium and enema already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. But since your belly is still distended, we want to be careful. We’ve ordered a CT scan of your abdomen to get a better look inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that right now. The scan will help us decide. You’re not having pain or vomiting, which is reassuring. It looks like your colon is very dilated, but not blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It shows your colon is markedly dilated, especially in the lower part, but there’s no blockage or free air. That means no perforation, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help your bowels move. You were supposed to do a prep for colonoscopy, but it didn’t work well. We’ll give you more bowel prep to clear things out safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still having bowel movements, just liquid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. The issue is the colon is stretched. We need to reduce the pressure. We’ll use a full bowel cleanse with Golytely to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a chest X-ray to check for any air under the diaphragm. Everything looks clear—no signs of a tear in the bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work is stable. White count is normal, no infection signs. Liver enzymes are a bit high, but we’ve seen that before. Nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been on bowel prep since yesterday. How’s your belly feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bloated, but no pain. I’ve been going to the bathroom a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The colon is slow to return to normal size. We’re planning a colonoscopy tomorrow to look inside, but we may not get all the way through due to how twisted your colon is.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if they can’t see everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Then we’ll do a virtual colonoscopy—a special CT scan that can spot any masses without needing the scope to go all the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better than surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No signs of cancer or blockage so far. This is more about managing chronic constipation and your colon’s size.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, we just finished the colonoscopy. We got to the ascending colon, but your bowel is very tortuous and the prep wasn’t complete. We couldn’t see the entire colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So did you find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No polyps or masses in the part we saw. The rest will be checked with the virtual colonoscopy today. But so far, no red flags.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today, once we get the virtual scan done. You’re stable, no pain, and your vitals are good. We’ll send you back to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—the virtual colonoscopy is complete. It’s limited because you couldn’t lie prone, but we don’t see any mass or stricture. No obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The main issue remains chronic constipation and your colon’s dilation. We’ll restart your usual bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go back to your facility today. Your constipation plan includes Miralax twice a day and Golytely if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You were on warfarin and Plavix, but we held them for the procedure. You’ll restart warfarin and Plavix at home, with Lovenox as a bridge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes and pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your usual meds are continued. Insulin, gabapentin, lidocaine patch, and morphine. We switched to IV morphine briefly to avoid slowing your bowels, but you’ll go back to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to avoid things that make constipation worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re adjusting your pain meds to balance comfort and bowel function. Try to minimize opioids when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your dysphagia means you stay NPO. All meds and nutrition through your PEG tube, as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s normal for me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Please follow up on the virtual colonoscopy results with your GI doctor. Keep up the bowel regimen and watch for swelling or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if your belly swells up or you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—your family is here, and transport is arranged. You’re doing well. Discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay consistent with your bowel routine and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your liver enzymes were mildly elevated, but stable. No action needed now, but your doctors will monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, as long as it’s not serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s likely chronic. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The virtual colonoscopy report just came in. No obstructing mass seen. Limited by fluid and positioning, but no concerning findings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue your bowel regimen and follow up with GI as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will give you your discharge meds list. Make sure your facility has all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, your leg swelling is chronic. No new clots. Just keep legs elevated when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Family says it’s from hanging leg over bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could contribute. Try to avoid that position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared for discharge. Transport is here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay on top of your bowel health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling very tired and not yourself today. Your family brought you in because you weren’t as alert as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mmm… can’t talk well. Feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard to speak. We’re going to help you. You were breathing fast and your blood pressure was low when you arrived, so we had to put a breathing tube in to protect your airway for a short time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tube… scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but it’s temporary. You’re off the ventilator now and doing much better. We found signs of a serious infection—your white blood cell count was high and you had low blood pressure, which we call septic shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? Where?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two places. First, your chest X-ray showed some lung changes, and we found pus in your breathing tube. The culture showed MRSA, a resistant staph infection in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: MRSA? Like a hospital bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We started antibiotics for that. The second infection is in your gut—Clostridium difficile, or C. diff. It causes bad diarrhea and comes from bacteria overgrowth, even without recent antibiotics in some cases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had loose stools… smell bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that matches. We’re treating both infections. For C. diff, you’ll get oral vancomycin. For MRSA pneumonia, you’ll get IV vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both? At same time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because they’re different infections in different places. We’ll monitor your kidney function since vancomycin can affect it, but your levels are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Kidneys? I had low creatinine earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was high when you came in—1.2, up from your baseline—because of low blood pressure. But after fluids, it’s coming down. Your kidneys are recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was very low—80 over 67—so we gave fluids and a medication called dopamine to support it. Now it’s stable without medicine. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sugar? I’m diabetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was 216 when you came in—elevated but not dangerous. We’re checking it four times a day and giving insulin as needed. It’s been well-controlled since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I feel better than this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your mental status has improved too. We were worried about a stroke, but your head CT was normal—no new bleeding or stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had strokes before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know. You’ve had past CVAs affecting your speech and movement. But today’s confusion was likely from the infection, not a new stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my belly? I’ve been constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your bowel regimen. You were on many medications, but with C. diff, we stopped Miralax and lactulose. We’re using docusate and monitoring your output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more enemas?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if needed. Right now, your bowels are active due to the C. diff, so we’re holding back on strong stimulants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Breathing easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We removed the breathing tube yesterday, and your latest chest X-ray shows improvement. No new pneumonia, though there’s still some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—from being less active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that clear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with deep breathing and movement. We’ve started physical therapy to help you sit up and move safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds? I take a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed them. We switched your antidepressant from duloxetine to paroxetine because it can be crushed. We stopped mirtazapine for now—it can make you too sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about blood thinners?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on warfarin for your DVT history. Your INR dropped to 1.9, so we increased your dose from 3 mg to 4 mg. It needs to be checked regularly after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Blood cultures came back negative—no bacteria in the blood. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So infection is clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your white count is coming down, you’re off pressors, and you’re alert. But you’ll need to finish the vancomycin—both IV and oral—for another week after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: At the nursing home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll go to extended care. They can give the IV antibiotics and continue your rehab. You’re stable but still need support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. You’re hemodynamically stable, tolerating tube feeds, and your infections are responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve simplified them. You’ll continue warfarin, clopidogrel, levothyroxine, gabapentin, and the new paroxetine. For bowels, docusate twice daily. And vancomycin—both oral and IV—for 10 more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, insulin lispro as needed. Your sugars have been good, but we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your care team will check your INR, kidney function, and complete the antibiotic course. We’ll also reassess your bowel regimen once C. diff is cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I’m going back to familiar staff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they know your history well. Keep doing your breathing exercises and stay hydrated. You’ve made great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll be in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in today because you had a fever. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever… low energy. Not eating well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure was low when you arrived—82 over 43. That’s why we’re keeping a close eye on you. We think you might have an infection in your lungs and possibly your urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs? I’ve had trouble before… Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of your history, we started strong antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—to cover resistant bacteria like MRSA and Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… antibiotics again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We also sent a urine test. It showed a lot of bacteria—Proteus stuartii. That’s causing your urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your other conditions. But we’re treating it. Your white blood cell count was very high—21.9—so your body is fighting hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows infiltrates in both lungs. It’s hard to tell if it’s pneumonia or fluid buildup, but we’re treating it as pneumonia for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on the trach mask… breathing okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen levels are good. We’ll keep monitoring. You’re in the ICU tonight for close watch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure is better—118 over 70. You’re not febrile anymore, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feel more alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The chest X-ray from last night shows some pulmonary edema—fluid in the lungs—likely from heart strain. But it could also be infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heart? I have atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your INR was high—4.0—so we held your Coumadin. Too high increases bleeding risk. We’re using metoprolol to control your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no blood thinner now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just paused. We’ll restart at a lower dose once your INR comes down. The antibiotics may have affected it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows the lung opacities are worse. We’re leaning more toward pneumonia than just fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ve switched to meropenem and ciprofloxacin for better Pseudomonas coverage. Vancomycin continues for MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cipro… I’ve taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll switch it to oral later. Also, your urine culture confirmed Proteus stuartii, sensitive to several antibiotics, so we’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my mouth? It’s sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have thrush—yeast infection. We’ve started nystatin swish and swallow. It should clear up in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count has dropped to 8.8—much better. You’re stable enough to move to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Less beeping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also, we’re placing a PICC line so you can get IV antibiotics at the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PICC line? In my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a small tube in a vein in your arm. It’ll stay in for the next 10 days of IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I still take oral vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Even though your recent C. diff test was negative, you’ll keep taking it for two weeks after finishing the other antibiotics to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugars are under 150. We’re using sliding scale insulin. We held your glargine during admission but can restart it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My back sore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stage III sacral ulcer is clean. Keep using morphine as needed, and the facility will do daily wound care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your chest X-ray today shows improvement in the lung opacities. The infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not home, but to extended care. You’ll finish 10 more days of IV antibiotics through the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take oral ciprofloxacin, continue oral vancomycin for two weeks after antibiotics, and restart Coumadin at 2.5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: INR checks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily at first. Call the nurse with results so we can adjust your dose until it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Metoprolol will continue. Your rate is good now—around 80. We’ve increased the dose slightly to 12.5 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep up with the antibiotics, wound care, and monitoring. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I know this has been a scary night. You had trouble breathing and turned blue, but the team helped you and you're safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mmm… blue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you stopped breathing for a bit. EMS suctioned a large mucus plug from your trach tube. That’s likely what caused it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Trach… stuck again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve had this happen before. We’re keeping a close eye on your secretions and suctioning as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs… okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan. You have patchy areas in your lungs—likely pneumonia or aspiration. We’re starting antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics… again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because we found signs of infection. We also took a sputum sample to check what kind of bacteria are there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No fever now. Your white count is a bit high, which supports infection, but you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sputum culture came back. You have Pseudomonas and Proteus in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudo… what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Two types of bacteria. Pseudomonas is common in patients with trachs. We’re adjusting your antibiotics to cover both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Need IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we placed a PICC line yesterday so you can get IV antibiotics safely. It’ll help you finish treatment at your care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PICC… okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found yeast in your urine. It’s likely from your catheter. We’re changing the catheter and starting fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeast? Like… fungus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a type of fungal infection. It’s treatable. We’ll give you oral medication for 13 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain… just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You had a big scare. Your body’s healing. We’re watching your oxygen and lungs closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest chest X-ray shows improvement. The collapse in your lower lobes is getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… breathing easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and your oxygen levels are stable on lower support. That’s a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Med changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your gabapentin for leg pain and baclofen for muscle tightness. Also adding senna for constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… stomach okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat urine culture still shows yeast, so we’re continuing fluconazole. No change there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to fully clear the infection. We don’t want it coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: INR?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 3.0 on admission—too high. We held Coumadin briefly. Now we’re restarting it at 4 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly at your trach site. The nursing staff noted some bleeding. We’ll monitor your INR closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Check again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll check it before you leave. You’ll need heparin shots until it’s above 2.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your chest X-ray today shows even more improvement. Your lungs are clearing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. We’re almost ready to send you back to extended care. You’ll finish antibiotics there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which ones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Levofloxacin and cefpodoxime for pneumonia, fluconazole for yeast. You’ll take them for several more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: PICC care?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your care team will flush it daily and give antibiotics through it. They’ll be trained before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sacral ulcer is stage I—stable. Keep turning regularly and we’ll send supplies for care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re discharging you today to extended care. You’ve recovered from the respiratory arrest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Continue all meds, especially the antibiotics and fluconazole. Watch for fever or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: INR check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, check INR on the scheduled day. Call your doctor for Coumadin dose adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your care team will coordinate follow-up. If anything changes, they’ll reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up the good work. We’ll send all instructions to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because of a fever and cloudy, milky urine. Do you understand so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… fever… urine… bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We think you have a urinary tract infection. Your white blood cell count is high, which means your body is fighting an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Foley… hurts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your catheter may have caused irritation. We noticed during transfer that the balloon might have inflated in the wrong spot. Urology is coming to replace it safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain… down there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that could be from the misplaced balloon. We’ll give you lidocaine gel to help with the discomfort before the new catheter goes in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started antibiotics called Cefepime to treat the infection. We’ll switch to Zosyn soon based on your history with resistant bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Antibiotics… like before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, similar. You’ve had Proteus infections before, and Zosyn works well against it. We’ll give it for 7 days through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect you’ll feel better in a few days. Your fever is already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The urology team replaced your Foley catheter using a small scope. It went well. Your urine is now yellow, not milky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more white stuff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No pus or clots now. That’s a good sign the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your urine culture back. It grew Proteus mirabilis. That confirms we’re on the right antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same bug… before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s sensitive to Zosyn, just like last time. We’ll finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… no resistance?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No resistance this time. You’re lucky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your sputum. We found Serratia marcescens, Proteus, and Stenotrophomonas. But you’re not running a fever, so we don’t think you have pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs… okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some haziness at the bases, but it’s likely atelectasis—collapsed air sacs—from not breathing deeply. Maybe a bit of pneumonitis from suctioning during the ambulance ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspiration?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But you’re not coughing or short of breath now. We’ll keep giving albuterol and ipratropium to help open your airways.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more antibiotics for lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped Vancomycin and Tobramycin. No need to treat what isn’t active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the same bibasilar opacities. No worsening. That supports it’s not pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lungs… stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a small bleed from your trach site the other night, but it stopped on its own. Oxygen levels stayed normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bleeding… serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. It could be minor irritation. The site looks clean. No recurrence in 3 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count has dropped from 23 to 8.5. That means the infection is clearing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good… almost done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. You’ve been afebrile for 48 hours. We’ll finish the Zosyn tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. The infection is treated. Blood cultures were negative, so no sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR today. It’s 3.2, which is therapeutic for your atrial fibrillation. We’ve restarted Coumadin at 4 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood thinner… safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, now that the acute issue is over. We held it the first day just in case of bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diabetes is stable. We increased your Lantus insulin from 32 to 35 units because your glucose was running high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sugar… okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Glucose is between 150–240. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow to extended care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to nursing home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We recommend follow-up with urology to discuss better long-term bladder management to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Catheter… problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Chronic catheters increase infection risk. Urology might suggest alternatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today is discharge day. Your infection is resolved, lungs are stable, and you’re back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medicines same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly. Lantus is now 35 units. Everything else is unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you… doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and follow up with urology when they call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your doctors here. You came in with a fever and some blood from your G-tube. We’re going to take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nodding, looks concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not saying much, but I see you’re following me with your eyes. That’s good. We’ve started some antibiotics because your white blood count is high and you had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gestures to throat, then points to G-tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the old G-tube had some blood coming from it and redness around the site. That’s why we brought you in. But we’ve checked with a CT scan, and there’s no leak or infection inside your belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. It shows some new shadows in your lungs, mostly at the bases. That could be pneumonia or from some aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Frowns, touches chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re treating it like pneumonia for now. You’re on strong antibiotics through your IV. We also did a mini-BAL to check what kind of bacteria might be in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Raises eyebrows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mini-BAL means we took a small sample from your airways. It helps us pick the right antibiotic. The first results show Serratia marcescens, which is a type of bacteria that can cause pneumonia in people with trachs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t worry. We’re already covering for it. Your labs also show your white count was very high—30.4—but it’s starting to come down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff. Even though you don’t have a colon anymore, we checked because of the antibiotics. Good news—it’s not active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods, seems relieved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your blood cultures are negative so far, which is great. No bloodstream infection. Your breathing is stable, and your oxygen levels are good on the trach mask.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gives a thumbs-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on antibiotics, but we might narrow them soon. The sputum culture also grew Pseudomonas and more Serratia. But your response is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down to 19.2—still high, but better. We’re switching from Zosyn to cefepime, which covers the bacteria we found better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks questioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a change in IV antibiotic. Same goal—clear the pneumonia. Tobramycin is being stopped because we don’t need it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re replacing your G-tube. It’s routine, but important. The old one had some bleeding, but the new one should help prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gestures to abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll use X-ray guidance to make sure it’s placed correctly in your jejunum. You’ll get a numbing gel around the site. No sedation needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube was replaced successfully. The new one is in the right spot, a bit farther in. Feeds have restarted and you’re tolerating them well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smiles slightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your white count is now 14.8—much better. Your pneumonia is improving. We’re going to narrow antibiotics again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks attentive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping cefepime and switching to levofloxacin by mouth through your G-tube. It covers both Serratia and Pseudomonas and you can take it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was checked. It’s a bit low at 1.8. You’re on warfarin for your atrial fibrillation. We’re adding heparin now to protect your heart until the warfarin kicks in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Points to arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the heparin goes through your IV. It works right away. We’ll stop it once your INR is in the safe range, around 2 to 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your INR is now 2.4—perfect. We’ve stopped the heparin. You’ll stay on warfarin at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gives thumbs-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lung X-ray is improving. The infiltrates are clearing. You’re breathing easier. We’ll keep you on levofloxacin for a full 14-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The wound care team checked your sacral ulcer. It’s a stage 2 pressure sore. They’ve given instructions for padding and turning every two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Touches lower back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the one. It’s not infected, just needs careful skin care. The nurses are helping with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is now 11.4—almost normal. Your fever is gone. You’re stable. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks pleased.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to extended care. You’ll keep taking levofloxacin through your G-tube for one more week to finish the 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your warfarin dose is being increased from 3mg to 4mg daily. The rehab team will check your INR daily and adjust it back down when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks questioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s just temporary—to get your levels up faster. They’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your son was called. He’ll get updates from the rehab team. Any questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shakes head no.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check. You’re doing well. No fever, breathing easy, labs improving. You’ll continue all your regular meds, plus levofloxacin for one more week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The G-tube is healing well. No more bleeding. Your pneumonia is resolving. You’re ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smiles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder: keep turning every two hours for your back sore. Take the antibiotics as scheduled. And the rehab team will manage your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods firmly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. You’ve made great progress. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Waves hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll miss you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand your GJ tube came out at the nursing home. We’re going to keep you here overnight to make sure everything’s stable before replacing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… tube out. Hurts leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you mentioned leg pain. We checked your vitals and labs, and you don’t have a fever or signs of infection. Your blood work shows your white count is a bit high, but we don’t see a clear source yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your leg. The swelling might be from lying on one side. We’ll also check your INR since you’re on warfarin for your atrial fibrillation. It was 1.9 on admission—slightly low, but we’re continuing your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Warfarin okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re keeping it the same for now. Your diabetes and thyroid meds are also continuing as usual. We’re giving you pain medicine through the tube site if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re scheduling the GJ tube replacement today. An interventional radiologist will do it using imaging to guide the new tube into place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll use numbing medicine around the site. You shouldn’t feel much. You’ll be awake but won’t need sedation. The procedure usually goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The team just replaced your GJ tube. It went well—no complications. The tube is in the right spot and can be used for feeding right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Leg still swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Your right leg and arm are both swollen. Since you have a history of clots, we recommend an ultrasound to check for a DVT. It might just be from positioning, but we want to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Need it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll arrange it soon. For now, your breathing is stable, lungs are clear, and your sacral ulcer looks clean. No signs of infection at the GJ site either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is pending, but we’re planning to discharge you today to extended care. Your GJ tube is working, and you’re stable otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Medicines same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your medications continue as before. The rehab team will manage your warfarin and check your INR regularly to keep it in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. Please watch for redness, swelling, or drainage at the GJ site. And the rehab team will follow up on the leg swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. You did well. The feeding tube is secure, and we’ll make sure your care continues smoothly at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge orders are ready. You’ll go back on your regular schedule of tube feeds, medications, and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Same meds, same feeds. Just make sure the rehab team checks your leg and your INR as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have the transport team get you ready. You should be at the facility by late afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Let the rehab team know if anything changes—especially with the leg or the tube site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in because they needed to replace your Foley catheter and you've been feeling unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been running a fever and my back hurts. They said something about infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we suspect a urinary tract infection from the catheter. That can sometimes lead to more serious infection in the bloodstream, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. We’ve started you on antibiotics through the IV to treat it. We also checked a chest X-ray because you had pneumonia recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did the X-ray show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s some blunting at the bottom of your lungs, likely from fluid or atelectasis—collapsed air sacs. It’s improved since your last scan, so that’s good. But we’ll keep an eye on your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been thirsty a lot too. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your labs show high sodium levels, which means you're a bit dehydrated. We’re giving you IV fluids to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. My diabetes—should I be worried about my sugar levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. Your sugars have been stable so far. We’ll adjust insulin as needed while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my heart—my rhythm’s been off before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have atrial fibrillation. We’re continuing your warfarin, and we’ll check your INR tomorrow to make sure it’s in the right range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I reviewed your urine culture results from this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they find what’s causing the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They grew Klebsiella pneumoniae, a type of bacteria. But the lab noted possible contamination, so we’re not 100% sure it’s the main culprit. Still, your symptoms and high white count suggest infection, so we’re staying on the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it resistant to any medicines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shows resistance to some, like cefazolin and ceftriaxone, but it’s sensitive to others—meropenem, nitrofurantoin, amikacin. We’re using an effective IV antibiotic based on this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. What about the pneumonia? Did they test for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a Legionella urine antigen test. It came back negative, which is reassuring. It doesn’t rule out all pneumonia, but it makes certain types less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I feel a bit better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your oxygen levels are stable, and your fever has gone down. That suggests the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back sore? The nurses mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a pressure ulcer on your lower back. It’s not new, and it’s not infected. We’ve noted it so the wound care team can manage it after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling this afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Fever’s gone, and I’m not as tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your repeat labs show your sodium is improving, and your white blood cell count is coming down. That means the infection is responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go back to the nursing home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’d like to keep you for a few more days to finish IV antibiotics and make sure you’re stable. We’ll switch to oral meds before discharge if you continue improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your sputum culture came back—just normal mouth bacteria, no serious lung infection. So we’re confident this is mainly a urinary source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The chest X-ray changes are probably from atelectasis—common when you’re not moving much. We’re encouraging deep breathing and mobility to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my blood? I remember being anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low, but it’s stable—no need for a transfusion. We’ll monitor it and manage it as part of your chronic conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well. We’ll switch you to oral antibiotics for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on the culture, we’ll use ciprofloxacin. It’s effective against the bacteria we saw, and it’s well-absorbed by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will I need another catheter change soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The current one is new and should last. Just make sure the nursing home checks it regularly and keeps the area clean to prevent another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs are stable, no fever for 48 hours. We’re discharging you today to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds should I continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your usual meds—warfarin, insulin, thyroid pill, blood pressure meds. Plus, finish the 7-day course of ciprofloxacin for the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the wound on my back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep it clean and dry. The nursing staff will reposition you regularly and use special padding to prevent worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I watch for any signs of the infection coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—fever, chills, back pain, or cloudy urine. If any of those happen, let the nurses know right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your INR should be checked in 3 days due to the warfarin. And your primary doctor will review your blood counts and kidney function in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re on the mend. The transport team will take you back to the facility in a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the doctors taking care of you today. You're in the hospital because your nursing home staff noticed you weren’t as responsive and had a fever. We’re going to figure out what’s going on and help you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you can’t speak, but if you can hear me, maybe just blink once for yes, twice for no. Can you hear me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blinks once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good, thank you. We’re very concerned because your white blood cell count is very high, and you had a lot of infected urine—about 2.5 liters—when we replaced your catheter. That likely caused your infection and drop in blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in septic shock, which means your body is fighting a serious infection. We’ve started antibiotics and fluids to help. You’re on medicine to support your blood pressure, but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Facial grimace, then slight nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know this is uncomfortable. We’ve given pain medicine through your patch, and we’ll keep you comfortable. Your kidneys are also affected—your creatinine was high at 1.6, but it’s already improving since we drained the urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium was high too—148—because of a lack of free water. We’re giving extra water through your feeding tube every few hours to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Eyes close briefly, then open—seems calmer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. Your blood cultures came back—they show Proteus bacteria, which is causing the infection. It’s sensitive to the antibiotics we’re using, so that’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from vancomycin to meropenem because it works better against this type of bacteria. You’ll stay on it for about two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Slight smile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. Johnson. You’re doing better. Your blood pressure is stable, and you’re off the medication that supports it. Your white count is coming down—from 40 to 28—so your body is fighting the infection well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is improving—creatinine is now 0.9. Sodium is 142, still a bit high, but we’re continuing the water flushes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Raises eyebrows slightly—seems alert.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your heart with an ultrasound. It looks strong—no damage. But we noticed your INR was low at 1.2, meaning your blood isn’t thin enough. You were on Coumadin, but it wasn’t given before admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So we’ve started heparin, then will switch to Lovenox until your INR comes up. You’ll restart Coumadin soon. We’ll monitor that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows low lung volumes, but no pneumonia. That’s expected given your condition. We’re doing breathing treatments to help keep your lungs clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your trach secretions are less purulent today—good sign the infection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smiles faintly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big day today—we’re going to place a PICC line so you can finish antibiotics outside the hospital. It’s a long-term IV in your arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The radiologist will use ultrasound to guide it. You’ll be awake but numbed. It’s safe and will help you get home sooner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks slightly anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it sounds scary, but you’ll be fine. We’ll be right there. It takes about 30 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully in your right arm. It’s working well, and we’ve started your meropenem through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Relaxed expression, slight nod.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are excellent—white count is now 6.9, lactate is normal, sodium is 136. Your kidneys are back to baseline. You’re no longer in sepsis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow to extended care. You’ll finish the 14-day antibiotic course through the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smiles broadly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back on Coumadin at 4 mg daily, but stop the Lovenox once your INR is above 2.0. The nursing home will check that weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing the water flushes through your feeding tube—four times a day—for now. They’ll adjust based on your sodium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blinks slowly—seems understanding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. You’re alert, afebrile, and all your labs are stable. We’re discharging you to extended care with the PICC line and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular meds—gabapentin, fentanyl patch, lansoprazole, and insulin. The wound care team will keep managing your sacral ulcer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Make sure they check your INR in a few days. Once it’s therapeutic, stop the Lovenox. And finish all the antibiotics—don’t stop early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods firmly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did really well. This infection was serious, but you responded quickly to treatment. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Smiles, eyes glistening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will take you in about an hour. Rest easy—you’re on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I know you can't speak, but I'm here to help. You were brought in because you weren’t responding at the nursing home. We’re going to take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was low and your oxygen levels were down. We think you have an infection, possibly from your lungs or your urinary tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started antibiotics through your IV. We also did a CT scan of your head—no stroke or bleeding. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some new shadows in your lungs. Could be pneumonia. But your urine was also cloudy and smelly—so we’re treating both possibilities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a trach mask for oxygen. We’ll keep monitoring your breathing and blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work shows your white count is high—sign of infection. Lactate is elevated too, which means your body isn’t perfusing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you’re in septic shock. That’s why your blood pressure dropped. We gave fluids and you’re a bit more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidneys are stressed—creatinine is up. But it’s likely from low blood flow, not permanent damage. We’re watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing broad antibiotics—meropenem and vancomycin—for now. We’ll adjust once we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the right lung collapse has worsened. We’re doing more suctioning through your trach to clear secretions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also increasing your breathing treatments. You’re still on antibiotics and fluids. Your blood pressure is better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good update—your latest labs show your kidney function is improving. Creatinine is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew Proteus mirabilis. That’s a bacteria we’ve seen in your past infections. It’s sensitive to meropenem, so we’ll keep that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping ciprofloxacin since we don’t think there’s a resistant strain this time. Vancomycin stays for broader coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are still negative after 48 hours—that’s reassuring. Less likely to be widespread bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking better. You’re more responsive—nodding when asked questions. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels are stable on the trach mask. The lung collapse is improving. We’re encouraged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line today so you can finish antibiotics outside the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in. It goes into a vein in your arm and up to a large vein near your heart. It’s for long-term antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The first X-ray showed it was too far in—into the right atrium. But we’ve pulled it back. Now it’s in the right spot—mid superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get meropenem every 8 hours and vancomycin every 12 through this line for 5 more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your INR today—it’s 3.8. That means your blood is too thin. We’re holding warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
